# A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development

Leming Shen    Qiang Yang    Xinyu Huang    Zijing Ma    Yuanqing Zheng
   Chris Xiaoxuan Lu ^(†)^(†)thanks: L. Shen, X. Huang, Z. Ma, and Y.
Zheng are with the Department of Computing, The Hong Kong Polytechnic
University, Hong Kong SAR, China. E-mail: leming.shen@connect.polyu.hk,
unixy-xinyu.huang@connect.polyu.hk, zijing.ma@connect.polyu.hk, and
csyqzheng@comp.polyu.edu.hk.^(†)^(†)thanks: Q. Yang is with the
Department of Computer Science and Technology, University of Cambridge,
Cambridge, UK. E-mail: qiang.yang@cl.cam.ac.uk.^(†)^(†)thanks: C. Lu is
with the Department of Computer Science, University College London, UK.
E-mail: xiaoxuan.lu@ucl.ac.uk.

###### Abstract

Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit powerful code generation abilities,
fostering agentic systems to automate edge AI application development.
However, existing agents typically operate via fixed agentic workflows
and predefined design spaces, struggling to handle rapidly evolving
demands of real-world scenarios (e.g., heterogeneous data modalities,
diverse task pipelines). Unlike prior systems that treat LLMs mainly as
code generators following rigid workflows, we fully exploit their
reasoning capabilities to allow agents to determine their own workflows
on the fly. To this end, we propose SE², a self-exploring and
self-evolving paradigm for adaptive edge AI development. Inspired by
human learning processes, we distill development into four atomic
operations (retrieve, reason, code, test), and empower agents to explore
workflows by dynamically and adaptively selecting an appropriate next
operation based on the current context. Extensive evaluations show that,
with adaptive workflows, the synthesized programs achieve up to 26%
higher accuracy and consume 28% lower resources than state-of-the-art
baselines, while maintaining superior adaptability to unforeseen edge AI
scenarios. This highlights the potential of reasoning-driven adaptive
agentic workflow in edge AI development.

###### Index Terms: 

Autonomous coding, LLM, agent

## I Introduction

Edge AI integrates AI techniques with heterogeneous mobile devices to
enable perception and actuation in real-world environments
\[[1](#bib.bib1), [2](#bib.bib2), [3](#bib.bib3), [4](#bib.bib4),
[5](#bib.bib5), [6](#bib.bib6)\], facilitating various applications such
as smart sensing \[[7](#bib.bib7)\], healthcare \[[8](#bib.bib8),
[9](#bib.bib9)\], and autonomous driving \[[10](#bib.bib10),
[11](#bib.bib11), [12](#bib.bib12), [13](#bib.bib13)\].

Developing such applications, however, relies on substantial domain
expertise among developers, who must analyze multimodal datasets, design
complex signal-processing pipelines, train AI models under diverse
constraints, and deploy them on heterogeneous mobile devices
\[[14](#bib.bib14), [15](#bib.bib15), [16](#bib.bib16),
[17](#bib.bib17), [18](#bib.bib18), [19](#bib.bib19),
[20](#bib.bib20)\]. Therefore, recent works \[[21](#bib.bib21),
[22](#bib.bib22), [23](#bib.bib23)\] build LLM-based agentic systems to
automate this process by leveraging LLMs’ code generation capabilities
and embedded domain expertise. These systems can translate user
requirements into executable edge AI programs based on handcrafted,
predefined agentic workflows, chaining modules such as knowledge
retrieval, task planning, code generation, and iterative refinement
\[[24](#bib.bib24), [25](#bib.bib25)\].

Fixed agentic workflows, however, often struggle to handle diverse edge
AI tasks in real-world scenarios
(Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development"),
left). In practice, edge AI tasks may span numerous mobile devices,
heterogeneous runtime environments, and dynamic performance and resource
constraints. As our study reveals
(§ [II-A](#S2.SS1 "II-A Limitations of SOTA Methods ‣ II Background & Motivation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development")),
even well-engineered agentic systems may struggle to accommodate such
variability, suffering from inflexibility, limited adaptability, and
high maintenance costs.

![Refer to caption](2611.01377v1/fig1_agent_human_comparison.png)

Fig. 1: Previous works handcrafted fixed agentic workflows to synthesize
programs. SE² autonomously explores and selects the next atomic
operation in program synthesis to meet diverse edge AI requirements.

The root cause is that fixed workflows are often constrained by the
specific assumptions and development experiences of workflow designers.
In practice, developers must explicitly enumerate workflow steps and
handcraft detailed prompts that regulate agent actions for each. As a
result, LLMs solely function as code generators following predefined
instruction flows. Yet, a key strength of LLMs remains under-explored:
their reasoning capabilities, i.e., the ability to make decisions in
response to dynamic context information. This gap motivates a key
research question: Can we harness LLMs’ reasoning capabilities to
autonomously construct adaptive workflows to meet the ever-changing
requirements of edge AI development? If successful, we could shift the
burden of workflow design from developers to AI agents, enabling more
flexible, adaptive, and scalable edge AI application development.

Moving toward such a self-exploring and self-evolving agentic paradigm,
we propose SE² that leverages LLMs’ reasoning abilities to autonomously
construct distinct workflows for various edge AI tasks. The core insight
is inspired by human learning processes, which involve iterative
knowledge acquisition, reasoning, practice, and reflection on
accumulated experiences. Likewise, an SE² agent explores its workflow
and evolves through iterations of reflection and exploration. Building
upon this vision, we distill edge AI development into four atomic
operations (retrieve, reason, code, test), which serve as meta building
blocks of agentic workflows
(Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development"),
right). The SE² agent autonomously selects the next appropriate atomic
operation based on its reasoning about the accumulated context, thereby
flexibly adapting to diverse edge AI scenarios. In addition, our SE²
agent evolves through self-reflection, rather than blindly adhering to
rigid workflows.

Nevertheless, three unique technical challenges needed to be addressed,
calling for novel design and implementation:

❶ Limited long-context reasoning capability. It is inefficient and
impractical to rely on a single agent to perform all the atomic
operations due to the limited long-context reasoning abilities of
current LLMs, even if they have large context windows
\[[26](#bib.bib26)\]. To tackle this, we adopt a coordinator-actor
agentic architecture, where a coordinator agent maintains a global view
and autonomously orchestrates four task-specific atomic agents, i.e.,
retriever, reasoner, programmer, and tester. As detailed in
§ [IV](#S4 "IV Detailed Design of SE2 ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development"),
this modular division of cognitive tasks effectively reduces reasoning
complexity over long contexts, fostering interpretable and traceable
decision-making.

❷ Lack of in-depth understanding of edge devices. Our feasibility study
(§ [II-B](#S2.SS2 "II-B Motivation & Feasibility Study ‣ II Background & Motivation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development"))
found that, even augmented with detailed device specifications, LLMs
still struggle to generate executable and performant edge AI programs.
The root cause is that LLMs lack runtime feedback from real-world mobile
devices. Consequently, the generated code often overlooks critical
operational semantics and hardware constraints (e.g., CPU architectures,
environment affinity, and memory allocation). To address this issue, we
propose a mobile runtime feedback mechanism that encodes grounded,
runtime-level semantics and conveys them to SE² agents as actionable
feedback, thereby closing the loop for optimization and iteration.

❸ Inability to adapt to evolving Edge AI tasks. Simply relying on
vanilla LLMs for decision-making cannot cope with the emerging and
evolving edge AI environments and tasks. To enhance the adaptability of
the coordinator as well as the atomic agents, we adopt reinforcement
fine-tuning (RFT) \[[27](#bib.bib27)\] with an ensemble
mutual-actor-critic strategy to improve their domain-specific reasoning
abilities. In addition, we design several continuously self-evolving
graders to assess the reasoning quality in edge AI contexts and provide
adaptive feedback to the RFT loop. This approach enables agents to
acquire new domain knowledge over time and agilely adjust their
workflows to handle unseen scenarios and edge cases.

We fully implement SE² and comprehensively evaluate it against 8 SOTA
baselines on an edge AI code-generation benchmark and three
representative multimodal edge AI applications (human activity
recognition, vision-language understanding, and autonomous driving),
spanning distinct modalities, reasoning complexity, and real-world
constraints. Extensive experiments reveal that baseline coding agents
cannot consistently generate performant code (40% success rate lower
than SE²). In contrast, SE² achieves up to 26% higher accuracy and 28%
reduction in resource consumption compared to SOTA methods, while
retaining superior generalizability across tasks. These results validate
the effectiveness of our reasoning-driven adaptive workflow construction
paradigm.

In summary, we make the following contributions:

![Refer to caption](2611.01377v1/fig2_rationale_agentic_workflow.png)

Fig. 2: A typical agentic workflow of existing work with detailed step 2.

- •
  SE² exploits LLMs’ reasoning capabilities to autonomously construct
  agentic workflows via self-exploration and self-evolution, addressing
  the limitations of fixed workflows in heterogeneous and evolving edge
  AI environments.
- •
  We design a reasoning enhancement framework featuring
  atomic-operation-level adaptive agentic workflow construction,
  runtime-grounded probe synthesis, and continual multi-agent reasoning
  evolution.
- •
  We implement and extensively evaluate SE² against eight SOTA agents on
  a public benchmark, three representative multimodal edge AI
  applications, and through a user study, demonstrating its superior
  accuracy and generalizability.

## II Background & Motivation

### II-A Limitations of SOTA Methods

By equipping LLMs with external tools (e.g., search engines), we can
build agents \[[28](#bib.bib28), [29](#bib.bib29), [30](#bib.bib30),
[31](#bib.bib31), [32](#bib.bib32), [33](#bib.bib33), [34](#bib.bib34),
[35](#bib.bib35), [36](#bib.bib36), [37](#bib.bib37)\] and design
agentic workflows guiding them to automatically solve complex tasks. As
shown in
Fig. [2](#S1.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ I Introduction ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development"),
an agentic workflow is typically a multi-step process where each step
receives the output from the previous step and produces a new
intermediate result. With carefully crafted prompts and tool usage rules
in each step, the agent can follow the workflow and synthesize various
executable edge AI programs for users.

To better understand the limitations (i.e., inflexibility, limited
adaptability, and high maintenance costs) of existing agentic workflows,
we conduct a preliminary study by reproducing three SOTA works for edge
AI development: AutoIOT \[[21](#bib.bib21)\], AutoEmbed
\[[22](#bib.bib22)\], and IoTPilot \[[38](#bib.bib38)\]. These methods
adopt predefined workflows involving background knowledge retrieval,
task decomposition, code generation, and debugging.

We ask them to develop a human activity recognition system (HAR) using
the multimodal XRF55 dataset \[[39](#bib.bib39)\] and repeat 100 times
to avoid randomness. We randomly remove data to simulate the modality
missing issue in real-world multimodal scenarios \[[40](#bib.bib40)\].
As shown in
Fig. [3(a)](#S2.F3.sf1 "In Fig. 3 ‣ II-A Limitations of SOTA Methods ‣ II Background & Motivation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development"),
only 32% of the synthesized programs of SOTA methods can be successfully
executed, and only 8% achieve comparable performance to a SOTA
handcrafted program. It is highly challenging to design a fixed,
one-size-fits-all workflow to adapt to unforeseen cases and accommodate
diverse edge AI requirements. Further inspection reveals heterogeneous
issues:

- •
  No unimodal verification: They do not verify the correctness of each
  code snippet for unimodal data processing before multimodal fusion.
  This is often discouraged in current multimodal application
  development pipelines \[[41](#bib.bib41)\].
- •
  No handling of missing modalities: 68% of the programs fail when
  certain data streams are absent due to the lack of elastic AI models
  for dynamic input handling \[[40](#bib.bib40)\].

To remedy the above as well as other heterogeneous failures, developers
have to repeatedly revise and refine their workflows by explicitly
listing regulations such as tool usage rules, edge-case handling advice,
and consistency checks. Maintaining such crafted rules for unseen
scenarios with diverse requirements becomes highly time-consuming and
error-prone.

![Refer to caption](2611.01377v1/fig3a_preliminary_study.png)

(a) Existing agentic systems typically fail to handle unforeseen
scenarios

![Refer to caption](2611.01377v1/fig3b_feasibility_study.png)

(b) Though feasible, most agents exhibited limited reasoning
capabilities

Fig. 3: Preliminary & feasibility study.

### II-B Motivation & Feasibility Study

Motivation. The root cause of these limitations is that the workflow
design and its underlying reasoning still heavily rely on human
developers, while LLMs are merely treated as code generators following
predefined instructions. As a result, these fixed workflows cannot adapt
to new tasks in practical real-world scenarios. Unlike SOTA methods, SE²
exploits LLMs’ reasoning abilities to enable agents to autonomously
optimize and adjust their own workflows in response to diverse goals.

We analyze over 30 agent-based code generation systems and find that
nearly all edge AI development workflows are composed of four atomic
agentic operations:

- •
  retrieve: An agent retrieves relevant domain knowledge from various
  data sources (e.g., databases, websites).
- •
  reason: An agent analyzes the current and past state based on the
  available information and makes inferences before selecting the next
  operation. This operation relies on the agent’s reasoning capabilities
  for decision-making.
- •
  code: An agent generates a Python¹¹ 1 We focus on Python since it is
  widely used for AI development \[[42](#bib.bib42)\]. code snippet.
- •
  test: An agent generates test cases, deploys the code snippet on the
  target mobile device (optional), executes and evaluates it, and
  records the evaluation results.

By enabling AI agents to autonomously select among these operations in
response to changing states, agentic workflows can be organically
constructed. Similar to next token prediction in LLMs, SE² instead
predicts the next atomic operation that drives the workflow forward.

Feasibility & Challenges. We build a single agent to test whether it can
construct workflows autonomously. We instruct the agent to synthesize a
multimodal HAR program and deploy it on a Jetson Nano board. We repeat
the test 100 times and find that certain constructed workflows can
sometimes generate executable edge AI code with satisfactory performance
after multiple trials. Notably, they share a similar and commonly
adopted structure: ”retrieve knowledge $`\rightarrow`$ generate code
snippets $`\rightarrow`$ test individually $`\rightarrow`$ multimodal
fusion $`\rightarrow`$ build elastic AI models $`\rightarrow`$
iteratively refine”. This implies that adaptive workflow is feasible.
Despite this feasibility, the overall success rate remains low (8/100),
comparable to directly running existing agents without modification.
Further in-depth analysis reveals that the failures stem from three
fundamental reasoning limitations
(Fig. [3(b)](#S2.F3.sf2 "In Fig. 3 ‣ II-A Limitations of SOTA Methods ‣ II Background & Motivation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development")),
precisely motivating the technical challenges that SE² need to overcome:

- •
  Long-Context Reasoning. 16 agents repeatedly execute the same action
  (e.g., searching dataset information) and fail to terminate. It is
  likely because a single agent performs all operations and accumulates
  increasingly long contexts, while LLMs inherently pay more attention
  to the earliest and most recent tokens in the context window, causing
  the agent to ”forget” previously executed steps \[[43](#bib.bib43)\].
- •
  Runtime-Aware Reasoning. Even with retrieved knowledge of the target
  device, 18 agents still produce error code either because the required
  runtime environments are incompatible with the device or because the
  resource consumption exceeds the device’s capacity. The reason is that
  the agent cannot access the device and thus lacks an in-depth
  understanding of its runtime environments \[[44](#bib.bib44)\] and
  resource constraints.
- •
  Outdated Models. 58 agents adopt overly general or outdated algorithms
  and AI models. This indicates that LLMs lack the reasoning
  capabilities to associate user requirements with SOTA edge AI
  algorithms and models.

To address these challenges, we design and implement a series of novel
techniques as detailed in
§ [IV](#S4 "IV Detailed Design of SE2 ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development").

## III SE² Overview

SE² aims to enhance and exploit LLMs’ reasoning abilities to dynamically
and adaptively construct agentic workflows, which translate user
requests into executable edge AI code on target devices. As shown in
Fig. [4](#S3.F4 "Fig. 4 ‣ III SE2 Overview ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development"),
SE² has two stages: 1) self-exploration for dynamic workflow
construction, and 2) self-evolution for runtime feedback and continuous
LLM tuning.

Self-Exploration. Given a user-requested edge AI task (❶), the
coordinator iteratively determines the next appropriate operation. At
each step, the coordinator analyzes the output from the previous
operation (❷), and generates the next atomic operation with detailed
instructions (❸). The corresponding atomic agent is activated (❹) to
execute the operation based on the instruction and generate an output
(❺), which is further sent to the coordinator (❻). Based on the
currently constructed workflow, the coordinator decides if extra
operations are required (❼) or concludes that the synthesized edge AI
program meets the user requirement with acceptable performance (❽). In
addition, SE² provides an interface for users to offer instructions for
workflow refinement (❾). As such, agentic workflows are autonomously
determined with minimal user intervention, offering enhanced flexibility
and adaptability. Note that to better interpret user intents, we can
orthogonally integrate existing arts (e.g., LLM-as-a-Judge
\[[45](#bib.bib45)\]).

![Refer to caption](2611.01377v1/fig4_system_overview.png)

Fig. 4: The overall architecture and workflow of SE² (with detailed
operations in step 3).

Self-Evolution. When the target device runs the generated code, the
mobile runtime feedback mechanism synthesizes a probe to extract runtime
semantics (e.g., memory allocation) as grounded, runtime-level feedback.
In parallel, our continuous LLM tuning paradigm records the mutual
feedback between the coordinator and atomic agents to incrementally
enhance their reasoning capabilities in the edge AI domain. As such, all
agents can continuously evolve, enabling them to adapt to unforeseen
scenarios and emerging edge AI knowledge.

## IV Detailed Design of SE²

### IV-A Hierarchical Coordinator-Actor Agentic Architecture

This module performs self-exploration by dynamically constructing
adaptive workflows. Due to LLMs’ limited long-context reasoning
abilities
(§ [II-B](#S2.SS2 "II-B Motivation & Feasibility Study ‣ II Background & Motivation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development")),
we propose a coordinator-actor agentic architecture, where a coordinator
agent orchestrates the self-exploring process by delegating distinct
tasks to four atomic agents: retriever, reasoner, programmer, and
tester. This design offloads the execution of atomic operations to
multiple task-specific agents for more efficient handling.

Challenge. In multi-agent systems, sharing contexts among agents often
leads to prohibitive costs \[[46](#bib.bib46)\], introducing a new
challenge: how to enable effective and efficient communication between
the coordinator and atomic agents while ensuring context coherence? To
address this, we design tailored prompts to regulate each agent’s
behavior and outputs.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Coordinator Prompt (P.1) for step transition includes:

- •
  Role & objective. We assign the agent a coordinator role and provide a
  task description that guides it to proactively orchestrate multiple
  agents for edge AI development.
- •
  Respond rules include descriptions of the four atomic operations and
  their selection rules. We task the coordinator with iteratively
  selecting an appropriate operation and activating the corresponding
  atomic agent for execution. We also introduce a quit operation that
  ends self-exploration if the generated code meets the user
  requirement. Importantly, beyond sticking to the general cycle of
  ”retrieve $`\rightarrow`$ reason $`\rightarrow`$ code $`\rightarrow`$
  test”, we encourage the coordinator to repeat any stage as needed,
  e.g., ”retrieve $`\rightarrow`$ reason $`\rightarrow`$ retrieve”.
- •
  Current state. Atomic agents’ activities are recorded during operation
  execution, serving as the current state and thereby enabling the
  coordinator to determine the next operation with enhanced contextual
  coherence.
- •
  Output specifications. To ensure that atomic agents can accurately
  interpret the operation, we stipulate that the coordinator only
  outputs three items: the operation name, a brief instruction, and
  relevant context information.
- •
  One-shot example. We provide a sample output to reduce ambiguity in
  task interpretation.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Atomic Agent Prompt (P.2) comprises four parts:

- •
  Role & objective. We also assign distinct roles to the atomic agents,
  along with descriptions of their jobs.
- •
  Operation execution rules. We encourage each atomic agent to
  proactively and repeatedly invoke relevant tools to obtain sufficient
  information or conduct thorough tests.
- •
  Output specifications. We stipulate that each atomic agent can only
  respond with a function_call with parameters to invoke a tool, or a
  message to quit the current operation.
- •
  Instruction & context information from the coordinator.

We instruct atomic agents to invoke tools until all necessary
information is gathered. Once a ”finished” message is generated, the
atomic agent’s activity is summarized and returned to the coordinator
for further decision-making.

Remarks. Through our coordinator-actor agentic architecture with crafted
prompts, the coordinator can autonomously explore appropriate atomic
operations based on its reasoning abilities. As such, agentic workflows
can be dynamically constructed to cope with unforeseen cases (e.g.,
modality missing), exhibiting enhanced flexibility and adaptability.

### IV-B Mobile Runtime Feedback Mechanism

This module facilitates self-evolution by providing runtime-level
feedback for decision adjustment. As detailed in
§ [II-B](#S2.SS2 "II-B Motivation & Feasibility Study ‣ II Background & Motivation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development"),
even with retrieved device information, some generated code remains
unexecutable, as SE² cannot directly access devices and lacks detailed
runtime signals during coding and testing. Thus, we propose a mobile
runtime feedback mechanism that obtains grounded, runtime-level
semantics as timely feedback.

Challenge. An intuitive way to extract runtime semantics is to apply
existing device profiling techniques (e.g., nn-Meter
\[[47](#bib.bib47)\]). However, they rely on rule-based scripts for
runtime monitoring, which are often insufficient for diverse and rapidly
evolving edge AI tasks. Instead, SE² synthesizes probe programs that
execute on the target device to extract only relevant runtime semantics.
Our insight is that the coordinator, overseeing the entire development
process, can serve as a supervisor for probe synthesis. The runtime
semantics collected by the probe are then fed back to atomic agents for
response adjustments. Specifically, we design: probe synthesis, semantic
alignment grading, and response adjustment.

Probe Synthesis. Different from general code generation, the purpose of
a probe is not to solve the coding task, but to extract latent runtime
semantics that agents cannot infer from textual device specifications.
Specifically, we prompt (P.3) the coordinator to synthesize a probe
program with two main considerations before on-device code execution:

- •
  Runtime semantics. Environment affinity reveals incompatibilities
  between library versions and hardware kernels. Memory dynamics reflect
  feasibility under runtime allocation and fragmentation patterns.
  Execution behavior exposes performance bottlenecks arising from
  scheduling, warm-up, and accelerator utilization. I/O feasibility
  verifies if essential data formats are supported.
- •
  Probe program requirements. Minimality ensures that each probe focuses
  on a single runtime factor, reducing confounding effects and enabling
  precise interpretation of observed behavior. Orthogonality prevents
  probes from blending unrelated concerns, preserving the diagnostic
  clarity for targeted adjustments. Executability guarantees that each
  synthesized probe can reliably run within the device’s native software
  stack and provide grounded evidence. Observability mandates that
  probes emit structured outputs, enabling the system to consistently
  extract useful runtime semantics.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Semantic Alignment Grading. Based on the runtime semantics obtained from
the probe, we need to judge if each atomic agent’s decision aligns with
the current device runtime and the edge AI requirement. Such semantic
alignment manifests in two aspects: 1) Local alignment: whether the
atomic agent’s response contributes to the agent’s current task, i.e.,
the coordinator’s instruction; 2) Global alignment: whether it
contributes to the coordinator’s overarching task, i.e., the user
requirement. We prompt the coordinator to assign two scores reflecting
the local and global alignment of each atomic agent’s response based on
six designed grading levels. In addition, we instruct the coordinator to
provide feedback for atomic agents to adjust their responses. For
example, ”The code should use a smaller batch size to reduce memory
usage and employ TensorRT to accelerate on-device inference”. As such,
the grading process for response $`r_{i}`$ is expressed as:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\{s_{l}^{i},f_{l}^{i},s_{g}^{i},f_{g}^{i}\}=\mathcal{L}(r_{i}\ |\ \mathcal{I}_{i},\mathcal{A}_{i},u,\mathcal{S})
``` |  | (1) |

where $`s_{l}^{i}`$ and $`s_{g}^{i}`$ are the local and global semantic
scores, $`f_{l}^{i}`$ and $`f_{g}^{i}`$ are the corresponding feedback,
respectively. $`\mathcal{I}_{i}`$ is the coordinator’s instruction.
$`\mathcal{A}_{i}`$ is the atomic agent’s activity record during
operation execution. $`u`$ is the user requirement. $`\mathcal{S}`$ is
the runtime semantics obtained from the probe. The scores and dialogue
will be stored in a dataset $`D_{a}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
D_{a}=\{(\mathcal{A}_{1},s_{l}^{1},s_{g}^{1}),(\mathcal{A}_{2},s_{l}^{2},s_{g}^{2}),\cdots\},
``` |  | (2) |

which will be further used for continuous tuning
(§ [IV-C](#S4.SS3 "IV-C Continuous LLM Tuning Paradigm ‣ IV Detailed Design of SE2 ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development")).

Response Adjustment. Considering both the current state and the feedback
from the coordinator, we prompt the atomic agent to adjust its response
and regenerate a better one:
$`\hat{r_{i}}=\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}_{i}\ |\ (f_{l}^{i},f_{g}^{i}))`$.
Note that we do not request agents to regenerate if the semantic score
exceeds four, as the response is sufficiently aligned with the intended
task, exhibiting only minor flaws that do not impact overall coherence
\[[48](#bib.bib48)\].

Remarks. We leverage the coordinator to provide guidance grounded in
mobile devices’ runtime constraints, enabling atomic agents to adjust
responses that better align with both the current operation and the
overall user requirement.

### IV-C Continuous LLM Tuning Paradigm

This module performs self-evolution by continuously tuning all the
agents to enhance their reasoning about evolving edge AI knowledge. We
focus on three aspects of enhancement: 1) The coordinator’s cognitive
reasoning to autonomously select the next appropriate operation. 2)
Atomic agents’ operation execution abilities. 3) The programmer’s
domain-specific reasoning abilities to interpret edge AI knowledge and
generate relevant algorithms. Though building a RAG database
\[[49](#bib.bib49)\] is promising, its timely maintenance demands
substantial domain expertise, and vanilla LLMs still require strong
reasoning abilities to comprehend the new knowledge
\[[50](#bib.bib50)\]. In contrast, we adopt a modified reinforcement
fine-tuning (RFT) \[[27](#bib.bib27)\] strategy to enhance agents’
reasoning abilities in edge AI without user intervention, which can
enhance LLMs’ reasoning capabilities in specific domains by tuning on
smaller amounts of data.

RFT Procedure. Unlike supervised fine-tuning \[[51](#bib.bib51),
[52](#bib.bib52), [53](#bib.bib53)\] that forces LLMs to generate
precise answers, RFT relies on a grader that scores generated responses,
followed by policy gradients to refine LLM parameters
\[[54](#bib.bib54)\]. RFT mainly consists of three stages: 1) Grader
design. A grader is created to score the quality of LLM outputs.
Generally, graders can take various forms, such as format checkers,
Python code, or even LLMs \[[27](#bib.bib27)\]. 2) Dataset construction.
We first prepare a question set, $`Q`$, with an expected answer set,
$`A_{e}`$, and input $`Q`$ into the LLM, $`\mathcal{L}`$, to obtain a
generated answer set, $`A_{g}`$. Accordingly, we prompt the grader,
$`\mathcal{G}`$, to score each answer. The tuning dataset, $`T`$, is
thus obtained as a set of questions, expected answers, generated
answers, and scores, $`s_{i}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{array}[]{l}a_{i}^{g}=\mathcal{L}(q_{i}),\quad\forall q_{i}\in Q\\
s_{i}=\mathcal{G}(q_{i},a_{i}^{g},a_{i}^{e}),\quad\forall a_{i}^{g}\in A_{g},\;\forall a_{i}^{e}\in A_{e}\\
T=\{(q_{i},a_{i}^{g},a_{i}^{e},s_{i}),\cdots\}\end{array}
``` |  | (3) |

3\) Fine-tuning. With the obtained training dataset, policy-gradient
updates (e.g., VPG \[[54](#bib.bib54)\]) are adopted for LLM tuning:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{g}=\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{s_{i}\in T}\nabla_{\theta}\log s_{i}\big|_{\theta}\hat{A},\quad\theta^{\prime}=\theta+\eta\cdot\hat{g}
``` |  | (4) |

where $`\hat{g}`$ is the policy gradient, $`|T|`$ is the dataset
cardinality, $`\theta`$ are LLM parameters, $`\hat{A}`$ are the
advantage estimates \[[55](#bib.bib55)\] based on the grader, and
$`\eta`$ is the learning rate. After several epochs, RFT enhances the
reasoning capabilities of LLMs by encouraging them to generate
high-scoring outputs more frequently while suppressing low-scoring ones.

Challenges. Directly adopting RFT in SE² faces two main challenges: 1)
Assessing the continuously evolving coordinator and atomic agents
necessitates multiple evolving graders. 2) Grading the programmer
demands complicated analysis of both the quality and performance of the
generated code across diverse edge AI algorithms. To tackle these
issues, we propose: 1) An ensemble mutual-actor-critic strategy to
enhance both the coordinator and atomic agents in a mutual-critique
manner. Our insight is that both the coordinator and atomic agents can
function as graders to criticize each other’s behaviors from distinct
perspectives. 2) A self-reflective grader to further critique the
programmer, considering both code performance and algorithm
specialization to the edge AI domain.

Fig. 5: Ensemble mutual-actor-critic strategy.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Ensemble Mutual-Actor-Critic Strategy. We augment the actor-critic
algorithm \[[56](#bib.bib56)\] with an ensemble updating strategy to
refine both the coordinator and atomic agents. As shown in
Fig. [5](#S4.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ IV-C Continuous LLM Tuning Paradigm ‣ IV Detailed Design of SE2 ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development"),
to update atomic agents, we treat the coordinator as the grader to
criticize atomic agent behaviors. In turn, to refine the coordinator, we
regard atomic agents as four separate graders, each criticizing the
coordinator from a distinct angle regarding their specific tasks. Thus,
both the coordinator and atomic agents can be mutually updated as
self-exploration progresses. Given the dataset $`D_{a}`$ in
Equ. [2](#S4.E2 "In IV-B Mobile Runtime Feedback Mechanism ‣ IV Detailed Design of SE2 ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development")
containing the scores for the atomic agents, their tuning processes are
expressed as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
s_{i}^{a}=\alpha\cdot s_{i}^{l}+\beta\cdot s_{i}^{g},\;\hat{g}=\frac{1}{|D_{a}|}\sum{\nabla_{\theta}\log s_{i}^{a}\big|_{\theta}\hat{A}},\;\theta^{\prime}=\theta+\eta\cdot\hat{g}
``` |  | (5) |

where $`s_{i}^{a}`$ is a linear combination of both local and global
semantic scores graded by the coordinator. To tune the coordinator, we
first design four tailored grader prompts for atomic agents to rate the
current atomic operation and instruction generated by the coordinator.
Taking the retriever as an example, the grading prompt (P.4) considers
both the correctness and necessity of the coordinator’s decision. An
ensemble score is then calculated via weighted aggregation:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{array}[]{l}s_{i}^{c}=\sum_{o\in\mathcal{O}}{w_{o}\cdot\rho_{o}},\quad s_{i}^{c}\in[0,5]\\
\rho_{o}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}s_{i}^{o}&\text{if the {coordinator}'s operation = }o\\
5-s_{i}^{o}&\text{otherwise}\end{array}\right.\end{array}
``` |  | (6) |

where $`o`$ is the current operation, $`w_{o}`$ is its assigned weight,
and $`s_{i}^{o}`$ is the score rated by each atomic agent. If $`o`$ does
not match the atomic agent’s operation, we compute the score as
$`5-s_{i}^{o}`$, as in this case, a higher score means that the atomic
agent considers its own operation to be more appropriate. The
coordinator is then updated using the ensemble score:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\quad\hat{g}=\frac{1}{|D_{c}|}\sum{\nabla_{\theta}\log s_{i}^{o}\big|_{\theta}\hat{A}},\quad\theta^{\prime}=\theta+\eta\cdot\hat{g}
``` |  | (7) |

Such an ensemble strategy allows bidirectional critique between the
coordinator and atomic agents during self-exploration, thereby fostering
reflection on accumulated context and enabling continuous, iterative
self-evolution.

Self-Reflective Grader for Edge AI. To further enhance the programmer,
we consider three main aspects:

- •
  Code quality includes syntax correctness and code smells, which are
  bad coding styles (e.g., no exception handlers) or potential
  weaknesses (e.g., deprecated packages) \[[57](#bib.bib57)\]. They can
  be scored by SOTA code quality inspectors.
- •
  Code performance is tested by prompting the tester to produce test
  cases and assess performance across multiple evaluation metrics. The
  tester is further prompted to assign a score to comprehensively
  reflect the results.
- •
  Algorithm specialization: Whether the programmer uses tailored
  algorithms to process sensor data. For instance, Butterworth filtering
  is commonly applied to Wi-Fi CSI data to suppress noise induced by
  non-human activities.

We prompt the programmer to first identify a list of sensor data
processing algorithms used in the generated code. For each algorithm, we
prompt (P.5) the programmer itself to grade it on a scale from 1
(completely mismatched) to 6 (fully tailored) based on how closely the
algorithm aligns with established, modality-specific methods. Higher
scores indicate stronger adherence to domain-relevant practices, and
lower scores reflect reliance on generic or unsuitable approaches. This
process exploits the self-reflection capability of the programmer, with
the reflection score further used in RFT to facilitate self-evolution.
Then the final score is:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
s_{i}^{p}=s_{i}^{q}+s_{i}^{cp}+\sum{\lambda_{j}\cdot s_{i}^{s_{j}}},
``` |  | (8) |

where $`s_{i}^{q}`$ is the code quality score, $`s_{i}^{cp}`$ is the
code performance score, $`s_{i}^{s_{j}}`$ is the $`j`$-th algorithm
specialization score with corresponding weight $`\lambda_{j}`$. Note
that all tuning is performed entirely offline, without interfering with
the online code generation.

## V Experiment Setup

### V-A Implementation

We fully implement SE² using o4-mini \[[58](#bib.bib58)\] as the
internal LLM for balanced reasoning and response latency. The initial
tool pool contains a Tavily-based search engine \[[59](#bib.bib59)\], a
Chroma-based database \[[60](#bib.bib60)\], a Python executor inside a
sandbox, a Pylint-based code quality inspector \[[61](#bib.bib61)\], and
a tool builder that allows agents to dynamically create new tools. We
carefully design all graders and adopt RFT following OpenAI’s official
guidelines \[[27](#bib.bib27)\]. We develop SE² with 5,288 lines of
Python code and deploy it on a local server. The generated code is
tested and deployed on various mobile devices, including portable
laptops, Jetson Nano, and Raspberry Pis, which are connected to the
local server via a router.

### V-B Evaluation Protocols

We use both a SOTA benchmark and three representative edge AI
applications for comprehensive evaluations. The benchmark provides a
controlled setting for measuring core capabilities, while the real-world
edge AI cases investigate the system’s effectiveness and adaptability in
practical scenarios. In addition, we conduct a user study to evaluate
the generalizability of SE², where we invite users to propose diverse
improvisational requirements (including unseen applications).

#### V-B1 Benchmark

We use IoTBench \[[50](#bib.bib50)\], a tailored benchmark to assess
LLMs’ abilities in generating IoT-relevant code. We filter out data
irrelevant to edge AI and augment the rest to 200 coding tasks. Each
task contains a ”task specification $`\rightarrow`$ edge AI code” pair
with curated test cases, each corresponding to a specific functional
requirement in the specification. We randomly split the augmented
benchmark into two parts: 20% for tuning and 80% for testing (RFT
requires less tuning data). The tuning and testing data have completely
different tasks.

#### V-B2 Multimodal Edge AI Applications

Considering different developing pipelines, data processing algorithms,
sensor modalities, and device heterogeneity, we select three
representative multimodal edge AI applications for evaluation:

❶ Human Activity Recognition (HAR) using the XRF55 dataset
\[[39](#bib.bib39)\], containing 42.9K samples and 55 action classes of
various human daily activities. Three modalities are involved: RFID,
Wi-Fi CSI, and mmWave. We request deployment on a Raspberry Pi with no
GPU and only 8GB RAM.

❷ Vision-Language Understanding (VLU) using the MMMU dataset
\[[62](#bib.bib62)\] for image Q&A. There are two modalities in the
dataset: image and text. We request deployment on a Jetson Nano board,
which has a different runtime environment from the local server where
SE² operates.

❸ Object Detection in Autonomous Driving (ODAD) using the aiMotive
dataset \[[63](#bib.bib63)\] in 176 scenes. This task is the most
complex, as it involves four modalities (1 LiDAR, 2 radars, 4 cameras,
and 1 GNSS+INS) with high dimensionality, necessitating advanced data
processing algorithms and AI models. Besides, we randomly remove some
data modalities to simulate the modality missing issue in real-world
scenarios.

#### V-B3 Baselines.

We compare SE² with 8 SOTA baselines:

- •
  General coding LLM: GitHub Copilot \[[64](#bib.bib64)\] suggests code
  snippets and functions following user instructions.
- •
  General coding agents (fixed workflow): MapCoder \[[65](#bib.bib65)\],
  AgentCoder \[[66](#bib.bib66)\], AgentSquare \[[24](#bib.bib24)\].
- •
  Coding agents tailored to mobile tasks (fixed workflow): AutoIOT
  \[[21](#bib.bib21)\], GPIoT \[[50](#bib.bib50)\], IoTPilot
  \[[38](#bib.bib38)\], AutoEmbed \[[22](#bib.bib22)\].

## VI Evaluation

### VI-A Benchmark Evaluation

#### VI-A1 Metrics

Code similarity: we convert code into embeddings that capture its
internal logic via CodeT5+ \[[67](#bib.bib67)\]. We compute the cosine
similarity between the embeddings of the generated and the reference
code (from IoTBench). A higher value indicates a stronger ability to
generate edge-AI-related code. Pass@k: measures the probability that at
least one of the top-k generated programs passes all functional test
cases \[[68](#bib.bib68)\]. A high value indicates SE² accurately
interprets tasks and passes more functional test cases from IoTBench.
Code quality: we use Pylint \[[61](#bib.bib61)\] to assess code quality.

#### VI-A2 Performance Comparison

As shown in
Fig. [6](#S4.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ IV-C Continuous LLM Tuning Paradigm ‣ IV Detailed Design of SE2 ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development"),
we find:

SE² can effectively generate functionally correct and performant code
tailored to edge AI following task specifications. On average, SE²
achieves an 11% higher code similarity score and a 17% higher pass@1
rate than baselines. The gain in pass@5 rate (10% $`\uparrow`$) is
relatively small because it has higher fault tolerance than pass@1.

Interestingly, general coding agents (GitHub Copilot, MapCoder,
AgentCoder) exhibit lower performance in terms of code similarity (14%
$`\downarrow`$) and pass@1 rate (25% $`\downarrow`$), indicating that
general coding agents are incapable of generating high-quality edge AI
programs. For instance, they all directly apply AI models on the raw
Wi-Fi CSI data without dedicated processing (e.g., Butterworth filtering
\[[69](#bib.bib69)\]) to remove noise induced by non-human activities in
HAR.

In contrast, IoT-tailored agents (AutoIOT, GPIoT, IoTPilot, AutoEmbed)
perform relatively better, owing to tailored designs such as RAG. In
addition, AgentSquare achieves comparable pass@5 performance to SE², due
to its iterative workflow optimization method. However, we find that it
requires much more time to generate performant code
(§ [VI-B](#S6.SS2 "VI-B Case Study on Edge AI Applications ‣ VI Evaluation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development")).

SE² significantly outperforms the baselines in code quality by an
average of 1.6 points. The reason is that our self-reflective grader
uses code quality as a grading metric. Thus, after RFT, the programmer
gains enhanced abilities to produce high-quality code while adopting
edge-AI-relevant algorithms. Notably, GitHub Copilot achieves higher
code quality scores than other baselines, as it uses tailored LLMs and
prompts for high-quality code generation, whereas other agents typically
rely on vanilla LLMs. In general, the superior performance of SE² stems
from its self-exploration abilities in adopting SOTA algorithms
dedicated to various edge AI tasks.

### VI-B Case Study on Edge AI Applications

#### VI-B1 Metrics

We repeat the test 100 times and calculate the average values of the
following metrics: Classification accuracy (HAR): the portion of the
correctly classified activities. Answer correct rate (VLU): the portion
of the correctly answered image Q&A pairs. Precision (ODAD): the portion
of the detected bounding boxes that are actually correct. Memory
consumption: the CPU RAM or GPU VRAM usage during code execution.
Inference time: the time used for processing a single multimodal data
batch on the target device. Execution success rate: the portion of the
programs that can be successfully executed. Wall-clock generation time:
the time from the user’s request to the final program synthesis.

#### VI-B2 Evaluation on HAR

We request that the multimodal HAR model be executed on a Raspberry Pi
(8GB RAM, no GPU). As shown in
Fig. [7](#S5.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ V-B1 Benchmark ‣ V-B Evaluation Protocols ‣ V Experiment Setup ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development"),
SE² outperforms baselines in terms of success rate (39% $`\uparrow`$)
and classification accuracy (26.5% $`\uparrow`$). We find that SE² first
generates a script to obtain the data dimension, which is not specified
in the requirement, indicating that SE² learns to fetch such important
yet missing information via self-exploration, rather than relying on
explicit workflow engineering by developers. In contrast, the baselines’
fixed workflows often get stuck in handling unspecified data dimensions.
Further, by decomposing the task into multiple subtasks, SE² can
independently generate, test, and refine code snippets for each,
ultimately achieving higher accuracy.

Most GitHub-Copilot-generated code cannot be executed, while executable
ones achieve only 34% accuracy on average. The reason is that GitHub
Copilot is designed for general-purpose coding and lacks specialized
designs. Thus, it cannot effectively produce tailored edge AI code. This
phenomenon is consistently observed across distinct edge AI tasks and is
exacerbated as the task becomes complex
(Fig. [8](#S6.F8 "Fig. 8 ‣ VI-B1 Metrics ‣ VI-B Case Study on Edge AI Applications ‣ VI Evaluation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development")
&
Fig. [9](#S6.F9 "Fig. 9 ‣ VI-B1 Metrics ‣ VI-B Case Study on Edge AI Applications ‣ VI Evaluation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development")).

Moreover, SE²-designed models consume moderate memory with acceptable
inference latency
(Fig. [7(c)](#S5.F7.sf3 "In Fig. 7 ‣ V-B1 Benchmark ‣ V-B Evaluation Protocols ‣ V Experiment Setup ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development")).
Though AutoIOT and GPIoT adopt thorough model optimization methods
(e.g., pruning \[[70](#bib.bib70)\]) to reduce memory cost to 2GB, the
resulting accuracy is much lower than SE². In addition, IoTPilot and
AutoEmbed sometimes achieve lower performance, likely because they are
more tailored to embedded tasks.

Lastly, SE² only needs 43 minutes for code generation, slightly
surpassing other agents that use fixed workflows. While GitHub Copilot
and GPIoT take only a few minutes with a few rounds of LLM calls, most
generated code is unexecutable. AgentSquare has a 13% lower success rate
and takes a much longer time (90 minutes) to generate executable code,
as it exhaustively searches over large module spaces.

#### VI-B3 Evaluation on VLU

We request to deploy the VLU model on Jetson Nano. Unlike the x86-based
PC where SE² operates, Jetson Nano uses ARM CPUs with a distinct runtime
environment for on-device deployment. Thus, agents must realize this
case and adopt an appropriate inference engine to ensure compatibility
with Jetson Nano.

As shown in
Fig. [8](#S6.F8 "Fig. 8 ‣ VI-B1 Metrics ‣ VI-B Case Study on Edge AI Applications ‣ VI Evaluation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development"),
SE² outperforms baselines in terms of both success rate (52.8%
$`\uparrow`$) and answer correct rate (23.9% $`\uparrow`$). Notably, the
success rate of baselines drops dramatically compared to HAR. After
analyzing their intermediate outputs, we find that they all ignore
runtime differences and repeatedly attempt to deploy x86-based models on
ARM-based Jetson Nano, as their fixed workflows ignore runtime
heterogeneity. In contrast, SE² realizes this issue by proactively
analyzing the runtime semantics obtained from the probe program. Then,
SE² creates a few more agentic steps to convert the model into a
platform-agnostic ONNX format \[[71](#bib.bib71)\] and use TensorRT
\[[72](#bib.bib72)\] compatible with Jetson Nano for model inference.
Besides, AgentSquare needs substantial time for workflow optimization
(Fig. [8(d)](#S6.F8.sf4 "In Fig. 8 ‣ VI-B1 Metrics ‣ VI-B Case Study on Edge AI Applications ‣ VI Evaluation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development")).
The accumulated context causes the agent to forget the device’s memory
constraints (4GB VRAM), producing models consuming over 10GB of VRAM
(Fig. [8(c)](#S6.F8.sf3 "In Fig. 8 ‣ VI-B1 Metrics ‣ VI-B Case Study on Edge AI Applications ‣ VI Evaluation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development")).

#### VI-B4 Evaluation on ODAD

We request deployment on an edge laptop with 16GB VRAM. This task is
highly complex as it involves four modalities of high-dimensional data.
Besides, we randomly remove some data to simulate modality missing
occurred in real-world autonomous driving scenarios. Agents ought to
account for this unforeseen case and build elastic AI models capable of
processing input data of varying sizes.

As shown in
Fig. [9](#S6.F9 "Fig. 9 ‣ VI-B1 Metrics ‣ VI-B Case Study on Edge AI Applications ‣ VI Evaluation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development"),
SE² outperforms baselines with a significant 50% higher success rate.
After reviewing its workflows, we find that though SE² initially creates
a model that fails to support elastic inputs, it discovers this flaw
during testing. SE² then agilely adjusts its workflow and modifies the
model to cope with varying input data sizes. Such developing pipelines
closely resemble humans, exhibiting remarkable adaptability of SE² in
handling unexpected cases. In contrast, the baselines repeatedly refine
the code by randomly adopting other data processing methods without
being aware of the crux. Consequently, they spend more time on debugging
and produce high-memory-cost models that fail to meet resource
constraints.

### VI-C Ablation Study

To separately test the impact of distinct modules, we conduct an
ablation study on multimodal HAR, with similar phenomena being observed
in other applications. Note that the superior performance of SE²
compared with the single-agent setting in
§ [II-B](#S2.SS2 "II-B Motivation & Feasibility Study ‣ II Background & Motivation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development")
has demonstrated the importance of our coordinator-actor agentic
architecture.

Mobile Runtime Feedback Mechanism. We test 3 ablation cases: SE², SE²
without the probe but replaced by a widely adopted runtime monitor
psutil \[[73](#bib.bib73)\], and SE² without any feedback.
Fig. [10(a)](#S6.F10.sf1 "In Fig. 10 ‣ VI-B2 Evaluation on HAR ‣ VI-B Case Study on Edge AI Applications ‣ VI Evaluation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development")
reveals that without full feedback, SE² experiences a significant 66%
drop in success rate and requires twice as long to generate executable
code. Without probe-collected runtime semantics, the coordinator cannot
provide useful feedback to atomic agents, and thus cannot identify if
the code is well aligned with the device’s runtime environment. Though
psutil can provide detailed runtime information, SE² often struggles to
extract content relevant to current coding subtasks, leading to a 1.5x
increase in synthesis time. These results highlight the importance of
our feedback mechanism in providing runtime semantics grounded in mobile
devices.

Continuous LLM Tuning. We test 4 ablation cases: SE², SE² without the
ensemble mutual-actor-critic strategy, SE² without the self-reflective
grader, and SE² without continuous tuning. In
Fig. [10(b)](#S6.F10.sf2 "In Fig. 10 ‣ VI-B2 Evaluation on HAR ‣ VI-B Case Study on Edge AI Applications ‣ VI Evaluation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development"),
all modules are crucial for retaining a high success rate and reducing
code generation time. Without the mutual-actor-critic strategy, the
coordinator and atomic agents cannot be mutually updated, resulting in
obsolete reasoning abilities when facing new edge AI knowledge and
tasks. Without the self-reflective grader, the programmer cannot reflect
on its generated algorithms and continuously evolve to produce
edge-AI-relevant code. These results show the effectiveness of our
continuous LLM tuning paradigm in enhancing agents’ reasoning abilities
for edge AI progressively.

### VI-D User Study for Generalizability Test

To assess the utility and overall user satisfaction, we conduct a user
study²² 2 Approved by our institution’s ethics review board (IRB).
involving 10 expert users and 10 non-expert users. Expert users have
rich experience in sensor data processing and AI technologies, while
non-expert users only possess basic knowledge of edge AI applications.
Importantly, to test the generalizability of SE², we did not limit the
tasks. Instead, users are encouraged to freely express their
requirements for developing various edge AI applications.
Table [I](#S6.T1 "TABLE I ‣ VI-C Ablation Study ‣ VI Evaluation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development")
lists the detailed background information of the participants.

#### VI-D1 Metrics

Overall code performance (OCP) evaluates the overall performance (e.g.,
accuracy, resource consumption) of the generated code; Code readability
(CR) measures the code clarity and structure; Generation efficiency (GE)
accesses how efficiently SE² is when producing the final code; Code
modularity (CM) judges if the code is properly modularized for easy
reuse and extension; User satisfaction (US) captures users’ overall
experience with SE². We ask users to rate these metrics on a scale from
1 (not at all) to 5 (completely).

#### VI-D2 Overall Performance

Users’ improvisational requests span a range of edge AI topics: mobile
sensing (40%), actuator control (40%), and personalized services (20%).
Experts often challenge SE² with more complex tasks (e.g., multimodal
emotion analysis) while non-experts tend to propose simple tasks (e.g.,
IMU-based HAR). In
Fig. [11(a)](#S6.F11.sf1 "In Fig. 11 ‣ VI-D3 Long-Term Evaluation ‣ VI-D User Study for Generalizability Test ‣ VI Evaluation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development"),
both experts and non-experts provide high scores (above 4.7) for OCP,
CR, CM, and US. Notably, nearly all users give CR full marks. After
analyzing the generated code, we attribute it to the hierarchical
agentic architecture, where distinct agents exploit their own reasoning
abilities to progressively generate modular code for various
functionalities. This process is akin to how humans divide a task into
multiple modules and generate modular code for each. Besides, experts
tend to rate GE lower than non-experts, as they are knowledgeable in
edge AI and have higher expectations for system performance. Despite
this, GE increases as system utilization grows
(§ [VI-D3](#S6.SS4.SSS3 "VI-D3 Long-Term Evaluation ‣ VI-D User Study for Generalizability Test ‣ VI Evaluation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development")),
benefiting from the continuous tuning paradigm. These results exhibit
the generalizability of SE² in exploring distinct workflows for diverse
edge AI tasks with enhanced user experience.

#### VI-D3 Long-Term Evaluation

We further ask expert users to join in long-term evaluations to test the
impact of the self-evolving paradigm.
Fig. [11(b)](#S6.F11.sf2 "In Fig. 11 ‣ VI-D3 Long-Term Evaluation ‣ VI-D User Study for Generalizability Test ‣ VI Evaluation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development")
shows that as user engagement increases over time, both GE and US rise
with a similar growth trend. As system usage time increases, the scores
graded by the coordinator and atomic agents gradually accumulate and are
used in mutual critique to enhance reasoning. Moreover, the retriever
progressively stores new knowledge in the local database for reference.
When new similar tasks occur, SE² can activate fast thinking to make
decisions rapidly without re-exploration, leading to shorter generation
times. Notably, though SE² initially tends to adopt hallucinated
algorithms, they are corrected by the feedback mechanism, and the
likelihood decreases as RFT progresses. These results demonstrate the
outstanding self-evolving abilities of SE² in handling diverse user
tasks and new edge AI knowledge.

## VII Discussion

Robustness and Reliability. SE² relies on LLMs, which may produce
hallucinations during multi-step reasoning. To mitigate this issue, SE²
incorporates Reflexion \[[74](#bib.bib74)\], which reflects on failed
attempts and evolves iteratively. The significantly higher execution
success rate
(§ [VI-B](#S6.SS2 "VI-B Case Study on Edge AI Applications ‣ VI Evaluation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development"))
validates the practical reliability of SE². Moreover, to further enhance
the robustness of SE² in detecting and recovering from mistakes, we plan
to integrate self-reflection techniques like ReAct \[[75](#bib.bib75)\]
as future work.

Generalizability. In the user study, we invited 20 participants with
distinct expertise in edge AI development. Admittedly, recruiting a
large cohort of more diverse participants could more comprehensively
evaluate both overall and long-term performance. In order to evaluate
external validity (i.e., generalizability to diverse user requirements),
we asked the participants to propose improvisational requirements. The
evaluation results
(§ [VI-D](#S6.SS4 "VI-D User Study for Generalizability Test ‣ VI Evaluation ‣ A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development"))
demonstrate the generalizability of SE² in handling diverse edge AI
tasks.

Vibe Coding vs. SE². Vibe coding refers to using LLMs to generate code
snippets purely from user instructions, without execution and
verification \[[76](#bib.bib76)\]. Users must manually design multiple
prompts and verify the correctness of all generated code. In contrast,
SE² provides an end-to-end solution that automatically translates user
requests into executable, runtime-compatible, and performant on-device
code. By fully utilizing LLMs’ reasoning abilities, SE² autonomously
determines and adaptively adjusts workflows for robust edge AI
development.

## VIII Related Work

Agents & Code Generation. By equipping LLMs with various external tools,
AI agents can automate complex tasks, such as phone manipulation
\[[29](#bib.bib29)\] and IoT data interpretation \[[77](#bib.bib77)\].
Many works build automated agents to synthesize various IoT programs.
For example, AutoIOT \[[21](#bib.bib21)\] generates IoT programs through
IoT knowledge retrieval and iterative refinement. AutoEmbed
\[[22](#bib.bib22)\] introduces a hardware-in-the-loop paradigm that
enables agents to flash generated code onto embedded devices. However,
developers must meticulously design and optimize agentic workflows to
ensure that agents can follow explicitly predefined guidance, limiting
their flexibility and adaptability. Instead, SE² exploits LLMs’ own
reasoning abilities to dynamically construct workflows.

Agentic Workflow Optimization. Some studies \[[25](#bib.bib25),
[78](#bib.bib78)\] focus on automated optimization of predefined
workflows to reduce human effort. For instance, ADAS
\[[25](#bib.bib25)\] and AgentSquare \[[24](#bib.bib24)\] regard
predefined workflows as combinations of various agentic modules (e.g.,
Chain-of-Thought \[[79](#bib.bib79)\] and Tree-of-Thought
\[[80](#bib.bib80)\]). Then, they perform an exhaustive search within
constrained spaces to identify the optimal combination that maximizes
performance. Yet, they still rely on fixed workflows bound by
developers’ experiences. Instead, drawing strengths from these arts, SE²
shifts the burden of workflow design from developers to LLM agents,
enabling more flexible and adaptive edge AI development. Notably, SE²
can also be orthogonally integrated with these arts for further
optimization.

## IX Conclusion

SE² is a self-exploring and self-evolving paradigm for adaptive edge AI
development. By fully exploiting the reasoning abilities of LLMs, SE²
agents can autonomously explore distinct appropriate workflows for
various edge AI tasks. In addition, our continuous LLM tuning paradigm
progressively strengthens agents to tackle evolving edge AI knowledge
and environments. Extensive evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness,
generalizability, flexibility, and adaptability of SE² in handling
diverse and evolving edge AI tasks. Looking ahead, we envision SE² as a
stepping stone toward more autonomous agentic systems capable of
adapting to dynamic environments as well as evolving through lifelong
learning and reflection.
````
